title: AI storytelling
content_html:
What You'll Do

In this project you're an author-illustrator working with AI as your helper. You'll invent a short story — a folktale, an adventure, or something funny — and use a text AI to help draft and polish the words. Then you'll use an AI image generator to illustrate your characters and settings. By the end you'll have a complete illustrated mini-story (3–6 pages) you can read aloud, print as a little booklet, or show as a slideshow.

The point isn't just a cute story — it's seeing how AI can be a creative partner that suggests ideas and draws pictures, while you stay the director, editor and decision-maker. You'll practise writing clear instructions (prompting), judging what the AI gives you, and shaping a story with a beginning, middle and end.

What You'll Need

  • A text AI — ChatGPT (chat.openai.com) for brainstorming, drafting and rewriting your story.
  • An image AI — Microsoft Designer / Bing Image Creator (designer.microsoft.com) for illustrations. Free accounts get a limited number of fast generations a day, then slow down.
  • Somewhere to write and build it — Google Docs or a notebook for drafting, and optionally Canva (canva.com) to lay out text and pictures into a booklet or slideshow.
  • A story plan with four boxes: Character, Setting, Problem, Ending.

Steps

  1. Warm up. Ask yourself: what makes a story fun to read, or a picture fun to look at? (Characters, surprises, colour, humour.)
  2. Plan your story. Fill in your four boxes. Example — Character: "Amina, a clever tortoise"; Setting: "a dry savanna during a drought"; Problem: "the animals can't find water"; Ending: "Amina remembers a hidden spring."
  3. Draft it with AI. In ChatGPT, turn your plan into a prompt: "Write a short 5-paragraph children's story about a clever tortoise named Amina who helps thirsty animals find water during a drought in the savanna. Use simple language for a young reader. End with a lesson about teamwork." Then ask it to tweak things: "Make it funnier," or "Add a mischievous hyena."
  4. Edit and make it yours. Copy the draft into a doc and change at least 3 sentences in your own words, add a personal detail, and fix anything that doesn't match your plan. The AI draft is a starting point, not the final answer.
  5. Split into scenes. Break your story into 3–5 short pages, a sentence or two each, ready to illustrate.
  6. Illustrate each scene. For every scene, write an image prompt with character + setting + action + style: "A friendly cartoon tortoise with a red bandana walking across a dry, cracked savanna under a hot sun, children's storybook style, bright colours." Generate it, and if it's not right, adjust the prompt ("make the tortoise smaller," "add animals in the background") and try again.
  7. Assemble it. Put your text and matching pictures in order in Canva, or arrange printed pages, to make the finished booklet or slideshow.
  8. Share it. Read your story aloud or show your slides.

Examples to Try

  • "Amina the Clever Tortoise": a 4-page story about solving a drought with memory and teamwork, in warm savanna-toned cartoon art.
  • "The Boy Who Talked to Matatus": a funny 5-scene Nairobi story about a boy whose matatu gives him advice, in bright comic style.
  • "Nia and the Missing Stars": a fantasy about a girl returning stolen stars with a magic telescope, in a dreamy blue-and-purple palette.

Tips

  • Unexpected result? Just rewrite the prompt — that's completely normal, not a failure.
  • Writing takes longer than you think and illustrating is quicker — don't spend all your time on page one.
  • Character looks different in each picture? That's because the image AI has no memory between separate requests. Fix it by using the same descriptive keywords (red bandana, cartoon tortoise) in every prompt.
  • Don't copy the whole AI story unchanged — the 3-sentence rule is what makes it yours.
  • Use specific, respectful words in image prompts — vague ones give odd results.

Think About It

  • What did the AI do well when writing your story, and what did you have to fix yourself?
  • How is asking an AI for a picture different from asking a human artist?
  • Why did the AI sometimes draw your character differently even with the same name?
  • Who is the "author" of your final story — you, the AI, or both?
  • How did a vague prompt compare with a detailed one? What does that teach you about giving instructions to AI?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Add one new illustrated scene that wasn't in your plan, with a line of dialogue for your main character.
  • Medium: Rewrite your story in a different genre (adventure → mystery, or fairy tale → sci-fi) using AI to brainstorm the changes, then make new illustrations.
  • Hard: Make a "choose your own adventure" version with at least two branching points where the reader decides what happens next — each path needs its own AI text and pictures.
